questions.question:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

"No sooner had she left the room when the lights went out."
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the use of the conjunction "**when**" in the third part of the sentence.
 
• The expression "**No sooner**" is a correlative conjunction that is always paired with "**than**," not "when."
 
• When a sentence begins with "No sooner," it requires **inversion**, where the auxiliary verb (had) comes before the subject (she). This part is correctly written as "**had she left**."
 
• To rectify the error, "when" must be replaced with "**than**" to complete the structure "No sooner... than."

Therefore, the correct answer is **3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"No sooner had she left the room **than** the lights went out."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "No sooner"** – This is the correct starting phrase for indicating that one event happened immediately after another.
 
• **Option 2: "had she left"** – This maintains the necessary inversion (Auxiliary + Subject + Main Verb) for sentences starting with negative adverbs.
 
• **Option 4: "the lights went out"** – This is a grammatically correct clause in the simple past tense, describing the second action.
 
• **Confusing Pairs:** Remember that "**Hardly**," "**Scarcely**," and "**Barely**" are the words that are paired with "**when**." (e.g., *Hardly had she left the room **when** the lights went out.*)

options.text: The way of the description by the teacher was imitated by the students.
The way of the description by the teacher were being imitated by the students.

questions.solution:

__
 
• Passive voice structure: The object of the active voice sentence becomes the subject of the passive voice sentence.
 
• In the active voice, the sentence is: "The students were imitating the way of the description by the teacher."
 
• To convert to passive voice: Place the object "the way of the description by the teacher" at the beginning.
 
• Change the active verb form "were imitating" to "was being imitated" (past continuous passive voice).
 
• Ensure the subject "the students" is preceded by the preposition "by" in the passive voice sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.
 
**Correct Sentence:** *"The way of the description by the teacher was being imitated by the students."*

• **Option 2: **"The way of the description by the teacher were being imitated by the students." – Incorrect subject-verb agreement (plural "were" is incorrect for singular "way").

questions.question: Which of the following policies were devised by Lord Dalhousie?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Doctrine of Lapse**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Doctrine of Lapse**: This policy was devised and implemented by **Lord Dalhousie** during his tenure as the Governor-General of India (1848-1856). It allowed the British East India Company to annex Indian princely states if the ruler died without a legitimate male heir. *Hence, this statement is correct.* 
• **Policy of Paramountcy**: Although the concept of paramountcy (British supremacy over Indian states) was strengthened during Lord Dalhousie's tenure, it was initiated earlier by other British officials. Dalhousie expanded its scope but did not devise the policy. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• **Subsidiary Alliance**: This policy was introduced by **Lord Wellesley** (1798-1805), not Lord Dalhousie. It required Indian rulers to accept British forces in their territories and pay for their maintenance, effectively reducing their sovereignty. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• **Policy of Non-Intervention**: This policy was followed during the early British rule in India, particularly under Warren Hastings, but was abandoned by later Governor-Generals, including Lord Dalhousie. Dalhousie was known for his interventionist policies. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• ***Therefore, the correct answer is Doctrine of Lapse.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Doctrine of Lapse:** 
• Introduced by **Lord Dalhousie** as a means to expand British control in India. 
• If a ruler died without a legitimate male heir, the state was annexed by the British East India Company. 
• This policy led to the annexation of several states such as **Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), and Awadh (1856)**. 
• The doctrine was highly controversial and led to widespread resentment among Indian rulers, contributing to the **1857 Revolt**. 
• **Policy of Paramountcy:** 
• Established British supremacy over Indian princely states. 
• Provided the British with the authority to intervene in the internal affairs of Indian states. 
• Expanded during Dalhousie's tenure but was not originally devised by him. 
• **Subsidiary Alliance:** 
• Introduced by **Lord Wellesley** in the early 19th century. 
• Required Indian rulers to accept British forces and pay for their maintenance. 
• Reduced the sovereignty of Indian states and brought them under British control. 
• **Policy of Non-Intervention:** 
• Followed by early British administrators like Warren Hastings. 
• Aimed at minimizing interference in Indian states' internal affairs. 
• Later abandoned in favor of more interventionist policies. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Impact of the Doctrine of Lapse:** 
• Created distrust and resentment among Indian rulers. 
• Contributed to the growing dissatisfaction that led to the **1857 Revolt**. 
• Highlighted the exploitative nature of British policies in India. 
• **Lord Dalhousie’s Reforms:** 
• Introduced modern infrastructure, including **railways, telegraphs, and postal systems**. 
• Focused on administrative efficiency and centralization. 
• Implemented the **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** for education reform.

questions.question: In which year did the National Stock Exchange began its operations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1994**__.

__
 
• The **National Stock Exchange (NSE)** of India began its operations in the year **1994**. It was established to bring transparency and efficiency to the Indian capital markets.
 
• NSE was incorporated in **1992** as a tax-paying company and received recognition as a stock exchange under the **Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**, in April 1993.
 
• The NSE commenced trading in the wholesale debt market segment in **June 1994**, followed by equity trading in **November 1994**.
 
• It was India's first exchange to offer a fully automated, screen-based electronic trading system, which provided easy accessibility and an efficient trading platform to investors.
 
• NSE has played a critical role in transforming India’s capital markets, enhancing market integrity, and promoting investor confidence.

__
 
• **National Stock Exchange (NSE):**

 
 
• The NSE is headquartered in **Mumbai, Maharashtra**, and is one of the largest and most advanced stock exchanges in India.
 
• The exchange's flagship index, the **NIFTY 50**, is used by investors in India and globally as a barometer of the Indian capital market.
 
• The NSE is regulated by the **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)**.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of NSE:**
 
 
• It introduced the concept of a **demutualized exchange** in India, separating ownership and management from the trading rights.
 
• NSE was the first exchange in India to offer a **derivatives trading platform**, beginning with the launch of index futures in **2000**.
 
• The exchange provides trading in various financial instruments, including **equities, debt, derivatives, and currency derivatives**.
 
 
 
• **Other Stock Exchanges in India:**
 
 
• The **Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE)** is the oldest stock exchange in Asia, established in **1875**.
 
• While BSE has historical significance, NSE has outpaced it in terms of trading volume and technological advancements.
 
 
 
• **Importance of NSE:**
 
 
• NSE has enhanced **transparency** by introducing electronic trading, reducing fraud and malpractices.
 
• It has made capital markets more **accessible** to retail investors, providing fair pricing mechanisms.
 
• The exchange is instrumental in **mobilizing savings** for economic development by providing a platform for investment in securities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SEBI and Market Regulation:**

 
 
• The **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** was established in **1988** and given statutory powers in **1992** to regulate the securities market in India.
 
• SEBI plays a key role in protecting the interests of investors and ensuring a fair and transparent trading environment.
 
 
 
• **Technological Advancements:**
 
 
• NSE’s trading platform is based on a state-of-the-art electronic trading system, capable of handling a large number of orders per second.
 
• The exchange provides **real-time price dissemination** to ensure informed decision-making by investors.
 
 
 
• **Global Recognition:**
 
 
• NSE is ranked among the **largest exchanges globally** in terms of trading volume.
 
• It has received multiple awards for its role in modernizing India’s capital markets and promoting financial inclusion.

questions.question: In which cell is the respiratory pigment haemoglobin found in humans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Red blood cells**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Haemoglobin** is a respiratory pigment found exclusively in **red blood cells** (RBCs) in humans. It is responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to tissues and carrying carbon dioxide from tissues to the lungs. 
• **Red blood cells** are specialized cells that lack a nucleus in their mature form, allowing more space for haemoglobin molecules. 
• Haemoglobin is a **protein** containing iron that binds to oxygen, forming oxyhaemoglobin, which is transported to various parts of the body. 
• RBCs are produced in the **bone marrow** and have a lifespan of approximately **120 days** before being broken down in the liver and spleen. 
• The presence of haemoglobin gives RBCs their distinctive **red color** and plays a vital role in maintaining the body’s oxygen supply. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Blood Platelets:** 
• Platelets, also known as **thrombocytes**, are small cell fragments involved in blood clotting. 
• They do not contain haemoglobin and their primary function is to prevent excessive bleeding by forming clots at injury sites. 
• Platelets are produced in the **bone marrow** and have a lifespan of **7-10 days**. 
• They play a critical role in wound healing and maintaining vascular integrity. 
• **Monocytes:** 
• Monocytes are a type of **white blood cell (WBC)** involved in immune responses. 
• They do not contain haemoglobin but are responsible for **phagocytosis**, where they engulf and destroy pathogens and cellular debris. 
• Monocytes differentiate into **macrophages** and **dendritic cells** once they migrate to tissues. 
• They are key players in both innate and adaptive immunity. 
• **Nerve Cells:** 
• Nerve cells, or **neurons**, are specialized cells responsible for transmitting electrical signals throughout the body. 
• Unlike RBCs, they do not contain haemoglobin and are not involved in oxygen transport. 
• Neurons consist of three main parts: the **cell body**, **axon**, and **dendrites**. 
• They play a vital role in coordinating bodily functions and processing sensory information. 
• **Important Points:** 
• **Haemoglobin** is composed of four protein chains and iron molecules, essential for binding oxygen. 
• It facilitates the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, ensuring proper cellular respiration and energy production. 
• A deficiency of haemoglobin leads to **anemia**, characterized by fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. 
• RBC production is regulated by the hormone **erythropoietin**, secreted by the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels.

questions.question: How do plants convey information about a touch from one cell to another?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By using electrical-chemical signals**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• Plants do not have specialized nerve tissues like animals. Instead, they rely on **electrical-chemical signals** to convey information between cells. 
• When a plant experiences touch, such as from an insect landing or wind blowing, it generates **electrical signals**, also called action potentials, that travel between the cells. 
• The movement of ions such as **calcium (Ca²⁺)** and other secondary messengers plays a key role in transmitting these signals. 
• These signals can trigger changes in cellular activities, such as the closing of stomata, the release of defensive chemicals, or the rapid movement of plant parts (e.g., the folding of leaves in the sensitive plant *Mimosa pudica*). 
• This process does not involve sound waves, color changes, or nerve tissues, which are mechanisms associated with animals or other systems. **Hence, the correct option is "By using electrical-chemical signals."** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Electrical Signaling in Plants:** 
• Plants use electrical signals, such as **action potentials** and **variation potentials**, to communicate within and between cells. 
• These signals are typically triggered by external stimuli like touch, wounding, or changes in light and temperature. 
• For example, the Venus flytrap uses electrical signals to snap shut its leaves when prey touches its sensory hairs. 
• **Role of Calcium Ions (Ca²⁺):** 
• Calcium ions act as **secondary messengers** in plant cells, helping to relay signals from the site of touch or damage to other parts of the plant. 
• Changes in calcium concentration within cells help activate specific genes or pathways for defense or adaptation. 
• **Plant Movement Responses:** 
• Touch-sensitive plants like **Mimosa pudica** exhibit rapid leaf movements in response to touch, a phenomenon known as **thigmonasty**. 
• Other movements, like phototropism (growth towards light) or gravitropism (growth in response to gravity), are slower but also involve chemical and electrical signaling. 
• **Misconceptions About Plant Communication:** 
• Plants do not have nerve tissues or produce sound waves for communication, unlike animals. 
• Color changes in plants, such as leaves turning yellow or red, are usually due to environmental factors or physiological changes, not a means of communication. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Thigmomorphogenesis:** 
• This is a long-term response in plants to mechanical stimulation, such as repeated touch or wind. 
• Plants that experience frequent mechanical stimuli often grow shorter and sturdier to withstand such forces. 
• **Defensive Responses:** 
• Plants can release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) as a chemical signal to warn neighboring plants of herbivorous attacks. 
• Touch can also stimulate the production of **defensive chemicals**, such as toxins or enzymes that deter herbivores. </ul

questions.question: "Taxila", the famous centre of learning, was the capital of which Mahajanapada in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gandhara**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Taxila**, an important center of learning in ancient India, was the capital of the Mahajanapada called **Gandhara**. 
• The **Gandhara Mahajanapada** was located in the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, covering parts of modern-day **Pakistan and Afghanistan**. 
• Taxila was renowned for its world-class **educational institutions**, attracting scholars and students from across the world, including notable figures like **Chanakya, Panini, and Jivaka**. 
• The city's strategic location on ancient trade routes, such as the **Uttarapatha**, made it a cultural and commercial hub. 
• Taxila flourished particularly during the **6th century BCE** to the **5th century CE**, under the influence of various dynasties, including the Achaemenids, Mauryas, Indo-Greeks, and Kushans. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Gandhara Civilization:** 
• The Gandhara region was an important cultural and political hub in ancient India, known for its **Gandhara art**, which combined Indian and Greek artistic influences. 
• The **Gandhara School of Art** is best known for its depictions of **Buddha** in human form, influenced by Hellenistic styles. 
• It was also a center for the spread of **Buddhism**, with numerous monasteries and stupas built during the reign of the Mauryan emperor **Ashoka**. 
• **Taxila University:** 
• Taxila housed one of the earliest known universities in the world, offering education in a wide range of subjects, including **medicine, law, politics, warfare, mathematics, and philosophy**. 
• It was unique in that it did not have a formal admission system; students came to study under specific teachers based on their expertise. 
• **Other Mahajanapadas:** 
• **Avanti:** Located in modern-day Madhya Pradesh, its capital was Ujjayini (modern Ujjain). 
• **Kamboja:** Situated in present-day regions of northern Afghanistan and parts of Central Asia, Kamboja was known for its warrior class. 
• **Kosala:** Located in modern-day Uttar Pradesh, its capital was Ayodhya, and it played a significant role in the early history of Buddhism and Jainism. 
• **Taxila’s Decline:** 
• Taxila's prominence declined after the invasions of the **Huns** in the 5th century CE, which led to the destruction of the city and its institutions. 
• The region subsequently lost its significance as a center of learning and cultural exchange. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Panini:** The ancient grammarian who authored **Ashtadhyayi**, the foundational text of Sanskrit grammar, was associated with Taxila. 
• **Chanakya:** Also known as **Kautilya** or **Vishnugupta**, the advisor to Chandragupta Maurya and author of the **Arthashastra**, is believed to have studied and taught in Taxila. 
• **Jivaka:** A renowned physician during Buddha's time, who studied at Taxila, is considered one of the earliest surgeons in history. 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Site:** The ruins of Taxila were declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in 1980, recognizing its historical and cultural significance. 
• **Archaeological Discoveries:** Excavations in Taxila have unearthed numerous artifacts, including stupas, coins, and sculptures, shedding light on its rich cultural heritage.
